The Math of Absorption, and Who This Isn’t For

In this article I ask people to talk about jealousy or God or death or childhood or money or sex or psychedelics or what to do when somebody wants to leave. Most people, intelligent, well adjusted in their thirties or forties, would rather talk for six hours about solar panels.

texts.241g-P10aP11r1:
I could go on and on, but the math is pretty clear by now. There wasn’t much of me left over for anybody else. So when I say someone might need to stabilize and do inner pl/ork before helping found a community, I’m not saying it from a mountaintop.

The problem is that, in a group of eight people, if two are in a sustained crisis mode, the group may end up spending most of its attention caring for those in crisis. However, in a group of eighty people, the same need can often be spread across lots of relationships and roles. A group can only absorb as much need as its members have free resource to meet.

texts.241g-P13n1P14mP15m:
There is a difficult paradox to consider. The need for new members in a small community is greater, but the ability of that community to tolerate the disruption of new members is less. Whether there are eight people in the community or eight hundred, someone still has to grow the food, fix the equipment, balance the books, watch the kids, and maintain the water system. The water well doesn’t care how beautiful a new member’s heart is.

Early on, members usually need to have more resource than need, and some skill to contribute, and a willingness to learn.

How to use the framing of “I don’t have the capacity to…” without it becoming a respectable way to exclude disabled people, poor people, less articulate people, people who don’t have the language of therapy at their fingertips, people who are simply not convenient – I don’t know. It’s not going to be solved by pretending it’s unlimited; that’s going to require actually making concrete criteria, allowing for outside review, allowing for re-visiting a “not now” decision, and all of that. And even then, the power is dangerous.
